subjects.introduction: To ask God for eyes that see is already to confess that one has been looking with borrowed sight. Bahá’u’lláh teaches that the divine Essence lies forever beyond the reach of the mind, and yet He calls each soul to gaze upon the signs of revelation with its own eyes and not with the eyes of others, as a Psalmist once asked for opened eyes and found the request bound up with obedience and longing [1]. The prayer for recognition therefore begins in humility, in admitting ignorance and asking to be made knowing, much as the Prophet was told to receive patiently before asking to grow in knowledge [2]. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of veils that must be burned away, of hearts purified, of a love whose fire outlasts separation and prison, and of a thankfulness that recognises even the capacity to respond as a gift. Such praying cannot stay inward. It learns to give up certainty about its own benefit and to turn toward mercy and forgiveness, as Jesus taught in the prayer He gave His disciples [3], until it reaches outward in prayer for the spiritual progress of others and in the daily practices of service. From here the way leads on into the knowledge and recognition of God, and into the wider life of prayer itself.

order.why: Begin with the relation between knowing God and recognizing the signs and Manifestations through which these writings speak of divine knowledge. The unknowability of the divine Essence remains beside the prayer for illumination. Read the appeals to fairness, independent sight and hearing, learning and teaching together. How might recognition deepen without becoming a claim to comprehend God? What distinguishes a living response to revelation from possession of an idea or a religious name?
